en: The Apadāna of the Elder Adhopupphiya Timiravagga, Chapter 4, Number 4 [Verse 1] I was a merchant in the city of Benares, and I possessed great wealth. I was a giver of alms and a donor of food to those who had gone forth. [Verse 2] At that time, there was a Buddha named Padumuttara, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One. He was the Teacher of the world, including its gods, a Buddha, a Fortunate One. [Verse 3] Having seen that Blessed One, the Great Sage, I offered him a single lotus flower with a devout heart. [Verse 4] When I had made that offering, the Buddha, the Great Sage, knowing my mind, spoke these words to me: [Verse 5] “O householder, you have given this lotus flower to me; because of this, you shall attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer. [Verse 6] Having heard the Buddha’s words, I was filled with joy and delight. Having paid homage to the Buddha, I departed from his presence. [Verse 7] After passing through many hundreds of thousands of eons, I was reborn in the human world, endowed with beauty and great splendor.

[Verse 8] In the city of Sāvatthī, I became a wealthy merchant. I was rich, possessed of great wealth, and a provider of food for the Saṅgha. [Verse 9] Then, having heard of the appearance of the Buddha, the Fortunate One, I went to the Jetavana grove, where the Teacher resided. [Verse 10] Having approached the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, I paid homage at his feet and sat down to one side. [Verse 11] Seated there, I addressed the Buddha, the Fortunate One: “I wish to go forth under the Dhamma of the Fortunate One. [Verse 12] The Teacher, the Fortunate One, out of compassion, granted me the going-forth. Having become a monk, I practiced the holy life under the Teacher. [Verse 13] By means of that root of merit, I attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer. Having seen the Truths, I took refuge in the Triple Gem. [Verse 14] For eighty-four thousand years I lived as a lay follower, observing the five precepts and honoring the Saṅgha. [Verse 15] Then, having heard of the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, the Fortunate One, I went to the Great Stūpa and honored it with flowers. [Verse 16] Having honored the stūpa with flowers, I paid homage and departed. After passing through many hundreds of thousands of eons, I was reborn in the human world. “That bhikkhu named Abhibhū was the foremost disciple of Sikhī;
he was of great power and possessed the threefold knowledge.”
He approached the Himavat mountains.
I too, O seer, am in the delightful, level expanse of the Himavat.
I dwelt in the immeasurables and then attained mastery over the supernormal powers;
like one born as a bird, I moved through the sky.
I took up residence upon the mountain;
having gathered adhopuppha flowers,
I returned to that mountain.
Having taken seven flowers,
I scattered them over his head as the Hero looked upon me.
I set out facing the east;
having reached the hermitage, I entered my dwelling.
Having taken a khāri-load,
I set out into the mountains;
there a python crushed me.
Of terrible form and great strength;
remembering my former deeds,
I passed away there.
In the thirty-first aeon from now,
because I offered that flower,
I have not known a state of misery.
This is the fruit of this flower-offering:
the four analytical knowledges... [and so forth].
“Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
In this way, it is said, the Venerable Elder Adhopupphiya recited these verses.
This is the fourth legend of the Elder Adhopupphiya.
